clue.text: Striker takes position for game’s critical moment

blocks.note: a match is struck to light it, so it is a striker
a point is a position, as in a point on a map

explanation.surface: A footballer moves into place just as the match reaches its decisive instant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striker' suggests a footballer, but here it is the humble match you strike.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis, the point that can win the whole contest is the tense decisive moment of play.

clue.text: Level lie, by the sound of it?

indicators.note: the phrase asks us to judge by how the word for a lie is spoken rather than spelt

blocks.note: a story is a fib told to deceive

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a flat statement could actually be a fib.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Level' looks like 'honest', setting up a contrast with lie, but it means a floor of a building.
explanation.definitionFit: A storey is one floor of a building, a horizontal tier or stage within it.

clue.text: Headline, one making a lot of noise?

definitions.text: one making a lot of noise

blocks.note: first meaning: a sensational newspaper headline in huge type

blocks.clueFragment: one making a lot of noise
blocks.note: second meaning: a person who shrieks loudly

explanation.surface: A front-page banner is pictured as something that shouts at readers.
explanation.definitionFit: Journalists' slang uses the word for a bold sensational banner, while literally it names anyone who shrieks.

clue.text: A tax collector ultimately beyond a two-dimensional icon

indicators.note: beyond places the following piece after the word it is set past
ultimately points to the very end, so only the final letter of collector is kept

blocks.note: VAT is value added tax, the UK sales tax

explanation.surface: A tax official seems to be placed past some flat image on a screen.
explanation.walkthrough: The collector's final letter sits beyond the second 'a', so the order is A, VAT, A, R.
explanation.definitionFit: An online user is represented by a small picture or figure standing in for them on screen.

clue.text: Fuel: one reeks after spillage

indicators.note: spillage scatters things, so the letters of the words before are spilt into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone smells strongly of fuel after a spill.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraffin oil burned in lamps, heaters and jet engines is a common liquid fuel.

clue.text: One girl edges away from another!

indicators.note: the edges are taken away, so the first and last letters of the other name are dropped

explanation.surface: One girl inches away from another, as if in a playground squabble.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' stands for a second girl's name, HANNAH; trimming its edges leaves ANNA.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna is a common female first name, so it is simply one example of a girl.

clue.text: Artificial image, latest captured

indicators.note: something captured is held inside, so one word is enclosed by the other

blocks.note: the latest is the last one so far

explanation.surface: A fake picture of the most recent event has been taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Something synthetic or false, like a fake smile or synthetic material, can be described this way.

clue.text: Six, say, tense before anaesthetic

indicators.note: before puts the first word's equivalent ahead of the second's

blocks.note: the perfect is a grammatical tense
an anaesthetic numbs, so it is a numb-er

explanation.surface: A patient is six times as nervous before the anaesthetic goes in.
explanation.walkthrough: NUMBER is read as numb-er, a thing that numbs. 'Say' signals six is an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Six equals the sum of its divisors 1, 2 and 3, the mathematical property defining this class of integers.

clue.text: Native abroad heading for mountainous country

indicators.note: abroad suggests being scattered far from home, so the letters are moved about
a heading is at the top, so only the first letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A local person travels overseas, making for a hilly nation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mountainous' seems to describe the country but only lends its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This Southeast Asian nation, once divided into north and south, is a sovereign state.

clue.text: Attractive area where I am deflecting bombs

indicators.note: bombs blow things apart, so the preceding letters are blasted into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone is fending off bombs in a pleasant-looking region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deflecting' looks like the operation but is part of the letters; 'bombs' is a verb meaning goes wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: The region around a magnet where its pull acts is a zone of attraction, punning on attractive.

clue.text: Theological studies topical in periodical

blocks.note: RE is religious education, a school subject

explanation.surface: Religious studies of the moment appear in a journal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Periodical' looks like a magazine noun but is used as an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something that happens again and again at intervals, repeating over time.

clue.text: Duck called for ape

blocks.note: a duck is a score of nought in cricket, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A duck quacked out to summon an ape.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a duck is a batsman's score of zero.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a shortened form of orang-utan, the great primate of Borneo and Sumatra.

clue.text: Vacant English politician, vacuous Tory

indicators.note: vacuous means emptied, so the inside of the next word is removed and only its outer letters stay

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
an MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A dim-witted Conservative MP from England is mocked as empty-headed.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A room or seat with nobody in it holds nothing, the same as being unoccupied.

clue.text: Unfortunately smellier, a French city

indicators.note: an unfortunate outcome is things going awry, so the letters fall out of order

explanation.surface: A sniffy traveller complains that a French port town smells worse.
explanation.definitionFit: This Mediterranean port is France's second largest urban area, on the southern coast.

clue.text: Laboratory experiment, content of chemical it must establish

indicators.note: content is what a thing holds inside, so the letters lie within the following words

explanation.surface: A lab test must establish what a chemical contains.
explanation.definitionFit: Dipping indicator paper into a liquid shows if it is acid or alkali, a classic school chemistry trial.

clue.text: Carrying Roo initially, Winnie the Pooh’s friend set off

indicators.note: carrying means holding something within, so one piece sits inside the other
initially points to the start, so only the first letter of the name is kept

blocks.note: the bouncy tiger in A. A. Milne's stories

explanation.surface: Tigger sets off with little Roo, the baby kangaroo, on his back, as in a scene from the Hundred Acre Wood.
explanation.walkthrough: The R goes in after the T of the friend's name.
explanation.definitionFit: To spark or start something, such as an alarm or a reaction, is to activate it.

clue.text: Drink teenager’s drunk

indicators.note: someone drunk staggers about, so the letters reel into a new order

explanation.surface: An adolescent has had too much to drink.
explanation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is': the teenager is drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Unfermented tea leaves brewed in hot water make this pale beverage popular in East Asia.

clue.text: Parent tries playing aces

indicators.note: playing with something means moving it around, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A mother has a go at a card game, playing her aces.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Aces' suggests playing cards but means experts.
explanation.definitionFit: Aces are experts, and masters of an art, especially great conductors, take this Italian plural.

clue.text: Teller of literary tale about popular hatter

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: the Miller tells a tale in Chaucer's Canterbury Tales

explanation.surface: A storyteller in a novel is wrapped around a well-liked hat-maker.
explanation.walkthrough: The Miller's Tale is one of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatter makes and sells hats, especially women's hats, which is exactly a milliner's trade.

clue.text: Crazy where ivy might climb?

blocks.note: first meaning: an idiom for driven mad or furious
second meaning, read literally: ascending a vertical garden partition

explanation.surface: A wild plant clambers somewhere unexpected.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone frantic or mad, while literally it is the direction a creeper grows on brickwork.

clue.text: A complex system observed before Durham’s opener bowled over

indicators.note: seen ahead of the next piece, so what comes first is placed in front
an opener comes first, so only the first letter of the place name is used

blocks.note: a maze is an intricate network of paths

explanation.surface: A cricket scene: Durham's opening batsman is bowled, as a complicated system was watched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opener' and 'bowled over' sound like cricket; Durham is an English county side.
explanation.definitionFit: To be knocked down figuratively by surprise is to be astonished or stunned.

clue.text: Slip down

blocks.note: first meaning: a mistake, especially a bungled line or shot
second meaning: soft light feathers or fibres

explanation.walkthrough: Together the two words read like falling over; they are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: A muffed line or shot is a blunder, while soft fibrous fuzz is like the downy feathers of a chick.

clue.text: Big cheese evidently satisfied mouser?

blocks.note: first meaning: an important, wealthy person
second meaning, read literally: a well-fed hunter of mice

explanation.surface: A cat that has caught a large cheese looks very contented.
explanation.walkthrough: A mouser is a cat that catches mice; a well-fed one is plump.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a rich, powerful businessman, and literally describes a plump, well-fed feline.

clue.text: Large animal like that filling waste basket

indicators.note: filling something means going inside it, so one piece is placed within the other

explanation.surface: Some big creature, or something like it, is stuffed into a rubbish bin.
explanation.definitionFit: The American buffalo is a massive hoofed beast of the prairies.

clue.text: One fish

blocks.note: first meaning: single, the only one

explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means only or single, and the noun is a flat seawater species eaten grilled.

clue.text: Greek philosopher, a leader on Rhodes TS Eliot translated

indicators.note: the leader is at the front, so only the first letter of the island is taken
translating changes a text's form, so the letters are converted into a new order

explanation.surface: A Greek thinker leads on the island of Rhodes, translating the poet T. S. Eliot.
explanation.definitionFit: The pupil of Plato and tutor of Alexander was a famous ancient thinker from Greece.

clue.text: Calm priest introduced to half-cut reverend

indicators.note: half cut away means the second half of the word is dropped
being introduced means being put inside, so one piece goes into the other

blocks.note: the full title, before half is removed
Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible

explanation.surface: A tipsy minister is soothed by a priest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for tipsy, but here it literally removes half the word; the priest goes in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To ease or soothe pain or anxiety is to lessen it, making someone calmer.

clue.text: Terribly pleased — passed!

indicators.note: terribly suggests something going badly wrong, so the letters are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: A student is thrilled at having passed an exam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed' looks like exam success but means time having gone by.
explanation.definitionFit: When time has gone by, it has slipped away, the sense of a period having run out.
